passages.t: He has risen; He is not here
passages.happening: When the Sabbath is over, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome buy spices to anoint Jesus' body. Very early on Sunday, the first day of the week, just after sunrise, they go to the tomb. On the way they wonder who will roll the heavy stone away for them. When they look up, it has already been rolled back. Inside they see a young man in a white robe sitting on the right, and they are alarmed. He says, “Do not be alarmed. You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has risen! He is not here! See the place where they put Him.” He tells them to go and tell the disciples and Peter that Jesus is going ahead of them into Galilee, and they will see him there, just as he told them. The women run from the tomb, trembling and bewildered. And because they are afraid, they say nothing to anyone.
passages.hearers:
The women came to finish a burial, not to see a miracle. Jews did not embalm the dead as the Egyptians did. Friends washed and wrapped the body and used spices and perfumed oil as an act of love. The Sabbath had stopped them on Friday evening, so they came at first light on Sunday with spices bought after the Sabbath ended. They expected a body.

In that world, a woman's word counted for less than a man's. Josephus, writing near the end of the first century, says that under Jewish law the testimony of women was not to be accepted (Antiquities 4.219). In the second century a critic of Christianity named Celsus mocked the resurrection as resting on the word of ‘a half-frantic woman’, as Origen reports in his reply. Yet all four Gospels agree that women were the first to find the tomb empty. Many historians think a story made up to convince people would hardly have chosen these witnesses. Mark had already said that these same women saw Jesus die and saw where he was buried (15:40, 47).

The young man in white is a messenger from God. White clothes in Mark mark the heavenly world, as at the transfiguration (9:3).

The first day of the week became the day Christians gather. Acts tells of believers meeting “On the first day of the week” to break bread (Acts 20:7). Justin Martyr, writing in the second century, says Christians assembled on Sunday partly because it was the day Jesus rose.
passages.ot:
Jesus had told the disciples three times that he would be killed and “after three days rise again” (8:31; also 9:31 and 10:34). He had also said, on the night he was betrayed, “after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee” (14:28). The young man simply reminds them: “just as He told you.”

The prophets had hoped for a day when God would “swallow up death forever” (Isaiah 25:8), and Daniel saw that “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake” (Daniel 12:2). Many Jews expected God to raise the dead at the end of time. No one expected one man to be raised in the middle of history, ahead of everyone else.
passages.hard:
Does Mark really end with frightened women saying nothing? In the two oldest complete Bibles that survive, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both copied in the 300s, Mark ends here at verse 8. In Vaticanus the copyist then left the next column blank, an unusual gap, and scholars still debate what that blank means. The Greek of verse 8 ends with a small word, gar, ‘for’: literally, ‘they were afraid, for’.

Did Mark mean to stop here? Many scholars think he did. On this view, the open ending is the point. The promise of verse 7 still stands, and the reader, who knows the women must have spoken in the end, is left to ask: will I tell? Other scholars think Mark's last page was lost, since the outer leaf of an ancient book was the easiest to tear away, or that he could not finish it. They point out that Matthew and Luke, who knew Mark, both go on to tell of meetings with the risen Jesus. Careful readers hold both views.

Either way, the good news is already plain in verse 6: “He has risen! He is not here!” And the women's silence did not last. The other Gospels tell how they went and told the disciples (Luke 24:9-11; John 20:18).

Their fear is not simply unbelief. In Mark, fear and amazement are how people react when God acts in power, as when Jesus calmed the storm and the disciples were “Overwhelmed with fear” (4:41).
passages.asks: Notice who the message is for. “Tell His disciples and Peter.” Peter, who denied Jesus three times, is named on purpose. The first word of Easter in Mark is for people who failed. Ask whether you believe that word is for you. And Mark's ending puts a question in your hands: the women were afraid to speak. What keeps you quiet about what God has done?

passages.t: The longer ending: appearances and unbelief
passages.happening: Most Bibles print verses 9 to 20 with a note or in brackets. They tell how the risen Jesus appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had driven out seven demons. She told the grieving disciples, but they did not believe her. Then he appeared in a different form to two of them walking in the country. They told the others, who did not believe them either. Later he appeared to the Eleven as they were eating and rebuked them for their unbelief and hard hearts, because they had not believed those who saw him risen.
passages.hearers:
Here is what the note in your Bible means, plainly. The two oldest complete Bibles end Mark at verse 8. Eusebius, the church historian of the early 300s, wrote that the accurate copies he knew ended there. Most later manuscripts include verses 9 to 20. They are old: Irenaeus quotes verse 19 around AD 180, long before those two great Bibles were copied. A few manuscripts have a different, shorter ending instead, and some have both.

Most scholars think verses 9 to 20 were added early by another writer. Their words and style differ from the rest of Mark, and they seem to gather events told in the other Gospels and Acts. A minority defends them as Mark's own. This is not a secret. It has been printed in the notes of Bibles for more than a century.

The events in these verses match what the other Gospels tell. John tells of Jesus appearing to Mary Magdalene (John 20:11-18). Luke tells of two disciples on the road to a village called Emmaus (Luke 24:13-35). Luke also says the disciples at first thought the women's words “seemed like nonsense” (Luke 24:11).
passages.ot: The great list of witnesses to the resurrection is in Paul, written in the 50s and handed on to him earlier still. Christ “was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve” (1 Corinthians 15:4-5). Paul adds that many of the witnesses were still alive.
passages.hard:
If these verses were not written by Mark, should they be in the Bible? Christians answer in different ways. Some churches receive them as part of Scripture because the church has read them for most of its history. Others read them as an ancient and valuable witness to what the early church believed, while building no teaching on them alone. All agree on one thing: nothing in verses 9 to 20 is needed for any Christian belief. The resurrection, the appearances, the sending out, and the ascension are all taught in the other Gospels, Acts, and Paul's letters.

Notice also how honest these verses are about the disciples. Again and again they do not believe. The first Christians did not pretend that they had been eager to believe. They had to be convinced.
passages.asks: Mary Magdalene was the first witness, and no one believed her. Ask whose testimony you are quick to dismiss because of who they are. And if you find it hard to believe, notice that the Eleven did too. Jesus rebuked their hard hearts, but he did not leave them. He came to them.

passages.t: The longer ending: sent into all the world
passages.happening: Jesus tells the Eleven, “Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature.” Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, and whoever does not believe will be condemned. Signs will go with those who believe: they will drive out demons, speak in new tongues, pick up snakes, not be harmed if they drink deadly poison, and lay hands on the sick so they get well. Then the Lord Jesus is taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God. The disciples go out and preach everywhere, and the Lord works with them and confirms the message by the signs.
passages.hearers:
These verses read like a summary of what Acts tells at length. The apostles drove out demons (Acts 16:18). They spoke in tongues at Pentecost (Acts 2:4). When a viper fastened on Paul's hand on the island of Malta, he “shook the creature off into the fire and suffered no ill effects” (Acts 28:5). They healed the sick. Notice that Paul did not go looking for the snake. It came at him by accident while he was gathering firewood.

The right hand of God is the place of highest honor beside a king. Jesus had told the high priest he would be seen “sitting at the right hand of Power” (14:62).
passages.ot: Sitting at God's right hand echoes Psalm 110:1, “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet,” which Jesus quoted in 12:36. Luke tells of Jesus being taken up in Acts 1:9: “a cloud hid Him from their sight.”
passages.hard:
Should Christians handle snakes or drink poison to prove their faith? No. Since the early 1900s, a small number of churches in the Appalachian region of the United States have handled venomous snakes in worship, reading verse 18 as a command. People have died from the bites, including leaders of the practice, and several states passed laws against it.

Verse 18 describes protection in the course of the church's mission, as when the viper struck Paul. It is not a test to set up. Jesus himself refused to test God. When the devil urged him to throw himself down and trust God to catch him, he answered, “It is also written: ‘Do not put the Lord your God to the test’” (Matthew 4:7), quoting Deuteronomy 6:16. Deliberately putting your life in danger to force God to act is exactly what Jesus refused to do. And no church should build a doctrine or practice on a verse from this disputed ending alone.

Verse 16 is also read differently. Christians disagree about how baptism and salvation are related. Notice that the verse says condemnation comes from not believing. It does not say that anyone who could not be baptized is lost. Because it belongs to the disputed ending, it is wise not to settle that question by this verse alone.
passages.asks: Whatever one thinks of who wrote these verses, their last picture is true to the whole New Testament: the risen Jesus sends his people out, and he goes with them. Ask where you have been sent: your home, your street, your work. Mark's Gospel began by calling itself the beginning of the good news (1:1). It ends with ordinary people carrying that news everywhere. The story is not finished, and you are part of how it goes on.
